summary.text: Couple the evolutions for masses \(n\) and \(n+1\) by representing the latter as the former plus one extra chip, whose position advances by the parity of the mass at its current site. A local classification of predecessors of the all-ones state, propagated by an invariant tracking the first non-unit cell, puts that chip at position \(n-2\) or \(n-1\) when mass \(n\) first stabilizes; it then takes exactly \(n-P\) further steps to reach the end.

full_proof.text:
Let all divisions below be integer divisions. Thus
\[
\left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil=\frac{m+1}{2},\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor=\frac m2.
\]
We prove the result by coupling the automata started with masses \(n\) and \(n+1\).

## 1. Infinite-function form of the automaton

It is convenient first to regard a configuration as a function
\(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), extended by zero beyond its last occupied cell. Define the one-step operator \(F\) by
\[
(Fg)(i)=\left\lceil\frac{g(i)}2\right\rceil+
\begin{cases}
0,&i=0,\\[2mm]
\left\lfloor\dfrac{g(i-1)}2\right\rfloor,&i>0.
\end{cases}
\]
This is exactly the cellular-automaton rule: cell \(i\) retains the ceiling of half its mass and receives the floor of half the mass of cell \(i-1\).

Write
\[
\delta_n(i)=\begin{cases}n,&i=0,\\0,&i>0,\end{cases}
\qquad
I_m(i)=\begin{cases}1,&i<m,\\0,&i\ge m.\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(\delta_n\) is the initial configuration of mass \(n\), while \(I_m\) is the stable configuration consisting of \(m\) unit cells. Let
\[
c_n(t)=F^t(\delta_n).
\]
In particular,
\[
c_n(0)=\delta_n,\qquad c_n(t+1)=F(c_n(t)).
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
F(I_m)=I_m. \tag{1}
\]
Hence, once the process reaches its target, it remains there.

We will repeatedly use the following no-holes property. Say that a configuration \(g\) is positive-prefix if
\[
g(i)=0\implies g(i+1)=0.
\]
Equivalently, after the first zero all later entries are zero. Every \(\delta_n\) has this property, and \(F\) preserves it. Indeed, if \((Fg)(i)=0\), then the nonnegative summand \(\lceil g(i)/2\rceil\) must vanish, so \(g(i)=0\). The positive-prefix property gives \(g(i+1)=0\), and then both terms defining \((Fg)(i+1)\) vanish. Consequently every \(c_n(t)\) is positive-prefix. We will also use the iterated form:
\[
g(i)=0\text{ and }i\le j\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(j)=0. \tag{2}
\]

## 2. Adding one unit of mass and following the extra chip

For a configuration \(g\) and a position \(p\), let
\[
(A_p g)(i)=g(i)+\mathbf 1_{i=p};
\]
that is, \(A_p g\) is obtained by adding one chip at position \(p\).

The key local arithmetic identity is
\[
F(A_p g)=A_{p+(g(p)\bmod 2)}(Fg). \tag{3}
\]
To see this, only cells \(p\) and \(p+1\) can be affected by adding one at \(p\). If \(g(p)\) is even, increasing it by one increases its retained ceiling-half by one and leaves its transmitted floor-half unchanged; the extra chip therefore remains at \(p\). If \(g(p)\) is odd, increasing it by one leaves the retained ceiling-half unchanged and increases the transmitted floor-half by one; the extra chip moves to \(p+1\). This is precisely (3).

Define the path \(P_n(t)\) of the extra chip recursively by
\[
P_n(0)=0,
\qquad
P_n(t+1)=P_n(t)+\bigl(c_n(t)(P_n(t))\bmod 2\bigr). \tag{4}
\]
Thus the path either stays put or advances one position at each step. In particular,
\[
P_n(t)\le P_n(t+1)\le P_n(t)+1. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(\delta_{n+1}=A_0\delta_n\), induction using (3) and (4) gives the fundamental coupling identity
\[
c_{n+1}(t)=A_{P_n(t)}c_n(t) \qquad(t\ge0). \tag{6}
\]

Suppose that at some time \(T\), the mass-\(n\) process is stable:
\[
c_n(T)=I_n. \tag{7}
\]
Then
\[
P_n(T)\le n. \tag{8}
\]
For if \(P_n(T)>n\), (6) says that \(c_{n+1}(T)\) is zero at position \(n\), but has the added chip and is therefore positive at position \(P_n(T)>n\). This contradicts the positive-prefix property of \(c_{n+1}(T)\).

By (1), equation (7) remains true at every later time. While the extra chip is at a position below \(n\), the underlying entry of \(I_n\) is \(1\), which is odd, so (4) makes the chip advance by one. Therefore, putting \(p=P_n(T)\), for every \(0\le j\le n-p\),
\[
P_n(T+j)=p+j. \tag{9}
\]
At time \(T+n-p\), the underlying mass-\(n\) configuration is still \(I_n\), and the extra chip has reached position \(n\). Thus (6) gives
\[
c_{n+1}(T+n-p)=A_nI_n=I_{n+1}. \tag{10}
\]

This also proves termination for every initial mass, by induction on \(n\). The mass-zero configuration is already \(I_0\). If the mass-\(n\) process reaches \(I_n\) at some time \(T\), then (8)–(10) show that the mass-\(n+1\) process reaches \(I_{n+1}\). Hence every stabilization time considered below exists.

## 3. A local analysis of the first non-unit entry

We need precise control of \(P_n(t)\) when stabilization first occurs. The following local observation is the main ingredient.

Let \(g\) be positive-prefix, and let \(i\) be its first entry not equal to \(1\):
\[
g(j)=1\quad(j<i),\qquad g(i)\ne1. \tag{11}
\]
Then at least one of the following holds:

1. \((Fg)(i)\ne1\);
2. \((Fg)(i+1)\ne1\);
3. \(g(i)=2\), all entries from \(i+1\) onward are zero, and
   \[
   Fg=I_{i+2}. \tag{12}
   \]

Here is the complete case analysis. If \(g(i)=0\), then the preceding entries are all \(1\), and the formula for \(F\) gives \((Fg)(i)=0\): for \(i=0\) there is no incoming term, while for \(i>0\) the incoming contribution from \(g(i-1)=1\) is \(\lfloor1/2\rfloor=0\). Thus case 1 holds.

Otherwise \(g(i)\ge2\). If \(g(i+1)>0\), then
\[
(Fg)(i+1)
=\left\lceil\frac{g(i+1)}2\right\rceil+
 \left\lfloor\frac{g(i)}2\right\rfloor
\ge1+1=2,
\]
so case 2 holds. It remains to suppose \(g(i+1)=0\). The positive-prefix property then says that every entry from \(i+1\) onward is zero. If \(g(i)=3\), then the retained contribution at \(i\) is \(2\), so \((Fg)(i)\ne1\). If \(g(i)\ge4\), then the amount sent from \(i\) to \(i+1\) is at least \(2\), so \((Fg)(i+1)\ne1\). Finally, if \(g(i)=2\), direct evaluation shows that the entries of \(Fg\) from \(0\) through \(i+1\) are all \(1\), and all later entries are zero: the earlier unit entries remain unit entries, cell \(i\) retains one, and cell \(i+1\) receives one. Hence (12) holds.

A useful consequence describes the configuration immediately before stabilization. Suppose that \(g\) is positive-prefix,
\[
Fg=I_n,
\qquad g\ne I_n. \tag{13}
\]
Then necessarily
\[
n\ge2,
\quad g(j)=1\ (j<n-2),
\quad g(n-2)=2,
\quad g(j)=0\ (j\ge n-1). \tag{14}
\]

To prove this, first note that some entry of \(g\) is not \(1\). Otherwise \(g\) would be identically \(1\), and so would \(Fg\), contradicting \((Fg)(n)=I_n(n)=0\). Let \(i\) be the first non-unit entry. Since \((Fg)(n)=0\), its retained term forces \(g(n)=0\), so \(i\le n\). In fact \(i\ne n\): if \(i=n\), then all entries below \(n\) are one, while \(g(n)=0\) and the positive-prefix property makes all later entries zero, giving \(g=I_n\), contrary to (13). Thus \(i<n\).

Apply the preceding three-way local analysis. Its first possibility is impossible because \((Fg)(i)=I_n(i)=1\). Its second possibility can only be compatible with \(Fg=I_n\) if \(i+1=n\). But in that event, the equation \((Fg)(i)=1\), together with the preceding unit entry when \(i>0\), forces \(g(i)=2\); then cell \(n=i+1\) receives \(\lfloor2/2\rfloor=1\), contradicting \((Fg)(n)=0\). Therefore only the exceptional third possibility can occur. It gives \(Fg=I_{i+2}\). Since the functions \(I_r\) are distinct for distinct \(r\), comparison with \(Fg=I_n\) yields \(n=i+2\), and (14) follows.

## 4. The lower bound on the chip position at stabilization

We now prove an invariant. For all \(n,t\), one of the following statements holds:

- \(c_n(t)\ne I_n\), and there is an index \(i\le P_n(t)+1\) such that \(c_n(t)(i)\ne1\); or
- \(c_n(t)=I_n\), and
  \[
  n\le P_n(t)+2. \tag{15}
  \]

At time zero this is immediate. For \(n=0\) and \(n=1\), the initial configuration already equals \(I_n\), and (15) holds because \(P_n(0)=0\). For \(n\ge2\), the entry at position zero is \(n\ne1\), so the first alternative holds with \(i=0\).

Assume the invariant at time \(t\). If \(c_n(t)=I_n\), then it remains equal to \(I_n\) by (1), while \(P_n\) is nondecreasing by (5), so the second alternative remains true at time \(t+1\).

It remains to consider the first alternative. Let \(i\) be the least index at which \(c_n(t)(i)\ne1\). By the invariant,
\[
i\le P_n(t)+1. \tag{16}
\]
Moreover,
\[
i\le P_n(t+1). \tag{17}
\]
Indeed, if \(i\le P_n(t)\), this follows from monotonicity. If \(i=P_n(t)+1\), then the minimality of \(i\) gives
\(c_n(t)(P_n(t))=1\), so (4) makes \(P_n\) advance by one, again proving (17).

Apply the three-way local analysis to \(g=c_n(t)\). In its first case, \(c_n(t+1)\) has a non-unit entry at \(i\); in its second case, it has one at \(i+1\). If the new configuration is not stable, these indices, together with (17), establish the first alternative of the invariant at time \(t+1\). If the new configuration is \(I_n\), a non-unit entry of \(I_n\) must occur at an index at least \(n\). Thus in the first case \(n\le i\le P_n(t+1)\), and in the second case \(n\le i+1\le P_n(t+1)+1\); either estimate implies (15).

In the exceptional third case,
\[
c_n(t+1)=I_{i+2}. \tag{18}
\]
But the mass-\(n\) process eventually reaches \(I_n\), as proved above, and both \(I_{i+2}\) and \(I_n\) are fixed by \(F\). Take any time at least both \(t+1\) and a time at which the process reaches \(I_n\). At that time the configuration is simultaneously \(I_{i+2}\) and \(I_n\), hence \(n=i+2\). Thus (18) is the target configuration. From (17),
\[
n=i+2\le P_n(t+1)+2,
\]
so the second alternative holds. This completes the induction proving the invariant.

In particular, whenever \(c_n(T)=I_n\), the invariant gives
\[
n\le P_n(T)+2. \tag{19}
\]

## 5. The upper bound at the first stabilization time

Suppose the process is not stable at time \(t\), but becomes stable at time \(t+1\):
\[
c_n(t)\ne I_n,
\qquad c_n(t+1)=I_n. \tag{20}
\]
The predecessor description (14), applied to \(g=c_n(t)\), shows that
\[
n\ge2,
\qquad c_n(t)(j)=0\quad(j\ge n-1). \tag{21}
\]
We claim
\[
P_n(t)\le n-1. \tag{22}
\]
If instead \(P_n(t)\ge n\), then by (6) and (21), the configuration \(c_{n+1}(t)=A_{P_n(t)}c_n(t)\) is zero at position \(n-1\), but is positive at position \(P_n(t)\), because of the added chip. This contradicts its positive-prefix property. Hence (22) holds.

If \(P_n(t)=n-1\), then the mass at that position is zero by (21), so its parity is even and (4) gives
\(P_n(t+1)=n-1\). If \(P_n(t)<n-1\), then (5) gives
\(P_n(t+1)\le P_n(t)+1\le n-1\). Thus in all cases
\[
P_n(t+1)+1\le n. \tag{23}
\]

Let \(T\) now be the *first* time at which \(c_n(T)=I_n\), where \(n\ge1\). If \(T=0\), then \(P_n(T)=0\), so \(P_n(T)+1=1\le n\). If \(T>0\), minimality says the process is not stable at time \(T-1\), and (23) applies. Therefore every first stabilization time satisfies
\[
P_n(T)+1\le n. \tag{24}
\]
Combining (19) and (24),
\[
n-2\le P_n(T)\le n-1. \tag{25}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
n-P_n(T)\in\{1,2\}. \tag{26}
\]

## 6. Exact relation between consecutive stabilization times

We next show that if \(T\) is the first stabilization time for mass \(n\), then the first stabilization time for mass \(n+1\) is exactly
\[
T+n-P_n(T). \tag{27}
\]
Equation (10) already shows that the mass-\(n+1\) process is stable by that time. It remains to show that it cannot stabilize earlier.

Suppose \(c_{n+1}(k)=I_{n+1}\) at some time \(k\). By the coupling identity,
\[
A_{P_n(k)}c_n(k)=I_{n+1}. \tag{28}
\]
We first deduce
\[
P_n(k)=n. \tag{29}
\]
If \(P_n(k)<n\), then evaluating (28) at the chip position shows that the underlying entry \(c_n(k)(P_n(k))\) is zero, because adding one there gives the target value one. The positive-prefix property then makes \(c_n(k)(n)=0\). But position \(n\) is not the chip position, while the right side of (28) has value one there, a contradiction. If instead \(P_n(k)>n\), then the right side of (28) is zero at the chip position, whereas the left side is at least one. Thus only (29) is possible.

Once (29) is known, (28), evaluated at every index, says exactly
\[
c_n(k)=I_n. \tag{30}
\]
Indeed, below \(n\) the target entries are one and no chip was added; at \(n\), the target one consists solely of the added chip, so the underlying entry is zero; and above \(n\) both sides are zero. By minimality of \(T\), (30) implies \(k\ge T\).

Assume for contradiction that
\[
k<T+n-P_n(T).
\]
Then \(0\le k-T<n-P_n(T)\). Since the mass-\(n\) configuration is fixed at \(I_n\) from time \(T\) onward, the chip-riding formula (9) gives
\[
P_n(k)=P_n(T)+(k-T)<n,
\]
contradicting (29). Hence every stabilization time for mass \(n+1\) is at least the quantity in (27), and (27) follows.

## 7. Return to finite list configurations

For completeness, we connect the function model exactly to the sequence in the statement. Given a finite list \(L\), let
\[
G_L(i)=
\begin{cases}
L_i,&i<\operatorname{length}(L),\\
0,&i\ge\operatorname{length}(L).
\end{cases}
\]
Appending zeros to a list does not change \(G_L\), and deleting trailing zeros does not change it either. If the list update is performed by taking the ceiling halves retained in each cell, appending a final zero, adding the list consisting of an initial zero followed by the floor halves transmitted from the preceding cells, and then deleting trailing zeros, direct evaluation at each index gives
\[
G_{\operatorname{step}(L)}=F(G_L). \tag{31}
\]
Starting from the one-element list \([n]\), induction on time therefore gives
\[
G_{S_n(t)}=c_n(t), \tag{32}
\]
where \(S_n(t)\) is the finite-list cellular-automaton state after \(t\) steps.

For \(n\ne0\), the initial list \([n]\) has no trailing zero, and every subsequent list has no trailing zero because trailing zeros are deleted at each update. The target list of \(m\) ones also has no trailing zero. Two finite lists with no trailing zero are equal whenever their zero-extended functions are equal: otherwise the longer list would have a final nonzero entry at an index where the shorter list has already become zero. Also,
\[
G_{[1,\ldots,1]}=I_m
\]
for the list of \(m\) ones. Consequently, for \(n\ne0\),
\[
S_n(t)=[\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{m\text{ entries}}]
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
c_n(t)=I_m. \tag{33}
\]
Thus the least stabilization time used to define \(a(n)\) is exactly the least \(T\) such that \(c_n(T)=I_n\). Existence was established in Section 2.

Now fix \(n\ge1\), and let \(T=a(n)\). By (27),
\[
a(n+1)=T+n-P_n(T).
\]
By (26), the final summand is either \(1\) or \(2\). Therefore
\[
a(n+1)=a(n)+1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
a(n+1)=a(n)+2.
\]
Equivalently, for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{1,2\},
\]
as claimed.
